title: Breville’s New Toaster Uses Optical Sensors to Measure Your Toast’s Doneness
gist: Wired gives Breville's $300 Eye Q optical-sensor toaster 5/10: the sensing works, but toast is no better or more even than conventional toasters, and units tested varied. The reviewer sees the real value in porting the optical tech to other Breville appliances.

insights.claim: Breville's Eye Q toaster replaces a timer with optical sensors that, per the company, scan the toast 10 times a second and stop toasting when it reaches the user's selected doneness; the 2-slot model costs $300 and the 4-slot $400.
insights.speaker: Joe Ray
insights.so_what: Sensor-driven closed-loop control is now reaching a mass-market appliance at a 4-5x premium to basic toasters.
insights.quote: uses optic sensors to scan your toast 10 times a second, the company says

insights.claim: Wired rates the Eye Q 5/10 because toast quality was merely comparable to a regular toaster, not superior, despite the $300 price.
insights.speaker: Joe Ray
insights.so_what: High-tech sensing did not translate into a better outcome, which caps the premium consumers should pay.
insights.quote: the quality of the toast it made was comparable, not superior

insights.claim: Testing found uneven results: tops darker than bottoms, seven doneness settings that were non-monotonic (setting six lighter than four), one unit that over-darkened light settings, and edges getting toastier as testing wore on.
insights.speaker: Joe Ray
insights.so_what: Quality control and calibration variance on a sensor-based product is a risk for early adopters; the reviewer suggests watching user comments first.

insights.claim: The reviewer wished Breville had built a toaster that toasts evenly and predictably rather than a new way to detect doneness, so paying $300 for a two-slot that does not get there 'stings'.
insights.speaker: Joe Ray
insights.so_what: Engineering effort went to a novel feature rather than the core job-to-be-done.

insights.claim: The Eye Q includes a sourdough mode that stops toasting while the center is lighter, a bagel/crumpet setting, a 'A bit more' button and an old-fashioned timer mode for Pop-Tarts and frozen waffles; sensors treat frozen bread the same, just taking longer.
insights.speaker: Joe Ray
insights.so_what: Feature breadth is a differentiator but not a toast-quality fix.

insights.claim: Toasters in general struggle to toast evenly regardless of price: America's Test Kitchen gives no toaster its Highly Recommended rating even in 2026, and Breville toasters are among its few Recommended picks but noted for uneven toasting.
insights.speaker: Joe Ray
insights.so_what: A stagnant category with a hard physical problem; incremental sensing has not solved it.
insights.quote: even in 2026, no toaster, no matter what the cost, gets their Highly Recommended rating

insights.claim: The author argues little has changed since 2016, when he called the toaster industry 'kind of a crap shoot' where spending more does not guarantee quality.
insights.speaker: Joe Ray
insights.so_what: Price is a poor proxy for quality in this category, weakening premium positioning.

insights.claim: A roughly 14-year-old, $70-today Cuisinart analog toaster with a doneness dial still satisfied the reviewer, and he ended up ready to go back to it after the Eye Q smoked a sourdough slice.
insights.speaker: Joe Ray
insights.so_what: Cheap, durable incumbents set a high bar for smart-appliance upgrade cases.

themes.theme: Optical sensing as a platform for Breville

insights.claim: The Eye Q's most interesting potential is the sensor tech itself, which could carry over to other Breville appliances, for example judging roast-chicken skin in a toaster oven.
insights.speaker: Joe Ray
insights.so_what: The toaster may be a low-risk testbed for vision-based doneness control across the premium cooking line.
insights.locator: The Eye Q's most interesting potential

insights.claim: The author imagines a future Breville oven pairing a probe thermometer with Eye Q-style optics to monitor the bird inside and out, cutting heat when skin is dark enough or adding a browning blast near the end.
insights.speaker: Joe Ray
insights.so_what: Sensor fusion (optical plus temperature) could enable automated cooking, a plausible next premium-appliance feature.
insights.locator: It could, say, drop the heat
